transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. Can you tell me what brings you in today?

Um… I guess it’s because at work I’ve had to be in front of people more, and now I keep noticing this uneven part of my face in photos. I kind of get stuck staring at it, even though people tell me they barely see anything.
How much has this concern about your facial asymmetry been affecting your daily life, such as causing you to avoid certain situations or feel very anxious?

It’s… been getting in the way more than I want to admit. I missed part of a planning deadline because I kept going over how I looked in the event materials. And now things like vendor calls or prepping for meetings take me longer than they should, because I get caught up in it.
Has this concern with your facial appearance caused you significant distress or made it hard for you to function in areas like work, social interactions, or personal relationships?

Yeah… it has. Mostly with work. I missed part of a planning deadline because I got caught up with how I looked in the event materials, and now even vendor calls or getting ready for meetings takes me longer than it should.
Do you find yourself spending a lot of time thinking about this facial asymmetry, or do you do things like checking mirrors, taking pictures, or comparing your face repeatedly?

Yeah… I do. Before I send event pictures or get on a vendor meeting, I’ll check my face on my phone camera a bunch, or retake photos. Sometimes I tilt my head so it looks less… off. I’ve asked a coworker if I look weird too. It can take longer than I mean it to, and then I’m behind on planning things.
Do you find yourself preoccupied with other parts of your appearance as well, or worry that other aspects of how you look are flawed?

Not really other parts, no. It’s mostly just… this one uneven part of my face. Since I’ve had to be more in front of people at work, I keep noticing it in photos, even though people tell me they barely see it.
